newsitem.title: USA: Separate trials are issue in Oklahoma City bombing.
newsitem.headline: Separate trials are issue in Oklahoma City bombing.

text.p: U.S. District Judge Richard Matsch began hearing evidence on Wednesday in a pre-trial hearing in which lawyers for the two defendants in the Oklahoma City bombing will argue for separate trials.
Matsch has set aside three days for the hearing.
Prosecutors are seeking the death penalty for defendants Timothy McVeigh and Terry Nichols, accused of the 1994 federal building bombing in Oklahoma City, which claimed 168 lives.
However, defence attorneys are expected to argue that evidence against the two is sufficiently different to warrant separate trials.
But prosecutors say two trials would be more expensive and time consuming than one, and the only way to paint a complete picture of the crime for the jury is to try both men together.
Matsch is expected to rule within two weeks on the motion to separate the trials.
Prosecutors argue that if any evidence should only be applied to one defendant it can be done so through the judge's instructions to the jury.

Attorney Bryan Stevenson and a retired criminal appeals judge from Texas, Charles Campbell, testified that the problem became acute during the penalty phase of a trial after the defendants were convicted.

Stevenson heads the Southern Centre for Human Rights, a non-profit group that represents defendants in capital cases. He testified that in the penalty phase a defence attorney must get the jury to focus on the life of the convicted man and that becomes harder when two people are tried together.
"They're fighting against one another to put themselves in the best light," Campbell testified.
Under cross-examination Stevenson conceded he was against the death penalty.
Prosecutors also want to spare victims and relatives of victims the pain of going through two trials. Cost is another factors, prosecutors say.

Separately, prosecutors filed with the court an affidavit from a paralegal who conducted a computer search on death penalty cases and found that for jointly tried defendants, 60 percent received life imprisonment while 40 percent got the death penalty.
In cases where defendants were tried separately, 62.5 percent received the death penalty and 37.5 percent got life terms.
The trial was moved to Denver as a result of widespread publicity and strong feelings in Oklahoma. It is expected to get underway early next year, although no date has been set.
